facts.fact: Pieter Bleeker described the species in 1851.
Its original name was Syngnathus heterosoma, published in Natuurkundig Tijdschrift voor Nederlandsch Indië, volume 2.
The type locality is Sambas in western Borneo, Indonesia.
The Catalog of Fishes lists three syntypes, with one of the museum specimens marked as uncertain.
The Catalog of Fishes now treats it as valid under the name Microphis heterosoma, following Haÿ et al. (2023); it was earlier listed under Doryichthys.
A 2023 integrative revision of Indo-Pacific freshwater pipefishes recognises Microphis as the single valid genus in place of six earlier genera.
The genus name Doryichthys comes from the Greek dory (lance) and ichthys (fish).
FishBase describes the body as eel-like.
It is a freshwater relative of the seahorse.
The body is very long and skinny, with a tiny tubular mouth at the end of an exaggerated snout.
The IUCN Red List classes it as Data Deficient.
It is known from only four specimens.
FishBase lists it as not evaluated by CITES.
Known only from the Sambas River in west Kalimantan and the Natuna Islands, Indonesia.
The four known specimens were collected in 1851 and the species is thought to be endemic to these locations.
The Catalog of Fishes gives its range as Kalimantan and the Natuna Islands, Indonesia.
A hobbyist video places it more widely, in parts of Southeast Asia and the Western Pacific.
The same video says it occurs in many regions, including landlocked lakes.
A retailer gives its origin as Southeast Asia.
FishBase classes it as a tropical, freshwater, benthopelagic fish.
A hobbyist video says it lives in streams, rivers and areas that can be influenced by estuaries.
It is offered in the aquarium trade; a UK retailer lists it as Longmouth Pipefish at 8 cm.
Before buying, ask the seller exactly what these individual fish are eating at that moment, especially whether they already take frozen food.
The presenter would not call it a beginner's fish, because of its specialised feeding rather than aggression or water needs.
The presenter says many freshwater pipefish in the hobby are captive bred in home aquariums.
The presenter says it does not need an extreme aquarium; no tank dimensions are given.
A mature aquarium is advised, since it holds more microscopic life as natural food than a newly filled tank.
Plenty of plants and structure, such as fine-leaved mosses, roots and branches, give it places to move through and hunt.
A retailer recommends a well-planted aquarium with hiding spots.
It is sometimes labelled brackish or saltwater, but the presenter says it can live in purely fresh water.
Once established and feeding, it is described as hardy and tolerant of a wide range of water parameters.
Keeping parameters stable matters more than copying the water of its origin.
Flow should be moderate, with calmer areas where it can hover, hunt and manoeuvre through plants.
A retailer advises pH 6.5–7.5, 22–26°C and dH 5–15, and stresses stable water.
It feeds on small crustaceans and insect larvae.
In the wild it takes tiny crustaceans, zooplankton, insect larvae and other suitably small prey.
In aquaria, live foods are the safest option, especially when the fish is first introduced.
Foods to try include baby and adult brine shrimp, Daphnia, copepods, mysids and other suitably small live foods.
Frozen foods may be accepted once the fish has settled in.
Do not expect it to survive on flakes and pellets.
A retailer says it feeds on small live invertebrates such as brine shrimp or daphnia.
It is a micro-predator that slowly approaches tiny animals and sucks them into its mouth.
It feeds slowly and deliberately, so fast or aggressive feeders can take all the food first, even if they are peaceful.
The presenter prefers a species-only aquarium for it.
If tankmates are needed, the presenter suggests microrasboras, Corydoras pygmaeus or smaller gobies.
Check that each fish is really getting enough food, rather than assuming so after seeing it take one brine shrimp.
A retailer describes it as shy, curious and not aggressive, but easily intimidated by boisterous tankmates or commotion.
In general biology it is ovoviviparous, and the male carries the eggs in a brood pouch under the tail.
Males carry the eggs and give birth to live young.
The female produces the eggs and transfers them to a brood area on the male, who protects them until the young are released.
In aquaria, raising the young is difficult because they need even smaller live foods, though the presenter says it has been done quite a bit.
